nodes.name: Brazil nut tree
nodes.desc: A towering canopy tree whose hard-shelled seeds are opened only by agoutis.

nodes.name: Kapok
nodes.desc: One of the tallest emergent trees. Its flowers feed bats and monkeys, and its leaves feed leafcutter ants.

nodes.name: Cecropia
nodes.desc: A fast-growing gap tree. Sloths browse its leaves, and ants live in its hollow stems.

nodes.name: Strangler fig
nodes.desc: Fruits through much of the year, so it feeds monkeys, birds and fish when little else is ripe.

nodes.name: Açaí palm
nodes.desc: Clusters of dark fruit feed toucans, tapirs and fish in flooded forest.

nodes.name: Floodplain plants & algae
nodes.desc: Floating meadows and algae in flooded forest that feed capybaras and fish.

nodes.name: Leafcutter ants
nodes.desc: Carry leaf fragments to underground gardens of fungus, which they eat.

nodes.name: Three-toed sloth
nodes.desc: Moves slowly through the canopy browsing leaves, and comes down about once a week.

nodes.name: Howler monkey
nodes.desc: Eats leaves, flowers and fruit, and announces its territory with a roar that carries for miles.

nodes.name: Agouti
nodes.desc: Gnaws open Brazil nuts and buries spares, planting new trees.

nodes.name: Lowland tapir
nodes.desc: Eats fruit and leaves, and spreads seeds across the forest in its dung.

nodes.name: Capybara
nodes.desc: The world's largest rodent grazes riverbank plants and rests in water to avoid predators.

nodes.name: Scarlet macaw
nodes.desc: Cracks open hard seeds and fruits high in the canopy.

nodes.name: Toco toucan
nodes.desc: Swallows whole fruit and drops the seeds far from the parent tree.

nodes.name: Tambaqui
nodes.desc: A big fish that swims into flooded forest to eat fallen fruit and seeds.

nodes.name: Ocelot
nodes.desc: A nocturnal hunter of agoutis, birds and small mammals.

nodes.name: Giant anteater
nodes.desc: Rips open ant and termite nests and licks up thousands of insects.

nodes.name: Boa constrictor
nodes.desc: Ambushes agoutis, birds and small mammals.

nodes.name: King vulture
nodes.desc: Finds carcasses by smell and opens them up for smaller vultures.

nodes.name: Red-bellied piranha
nodes.desc: Hunts fish in groups and scavenges dead animals in the river.

nodes.name: Giant otter
nodes.desc: Hunts fish in family groups along river banks.

nodes.name: Arapaima
nodes.desc: One of the largest freshwater fish. It breathes air and eats other fish.

nodes.name: Osprey (winter visitor)
nodes.desc: Spends the northern winter fishing Amazon rivers and lakes, then flies north to breed. Ospreys nesting at Yellowstone belong to the same migratory population.

nodes.name: Jaguar
nodes.desc: Hunts capybaras, tapirs, sloths and caimans, with a bite strong enough to crush skulls and shells.

nodes.name: Harpy eagle
nodes.desc: Plucks sloths and monkeys from the canopy with enormous talons.

nodes.name: Black caiman
nodes.desc: The largest predator in the flooded forest, eating fish, capybaras and anything else it can ambush.

nodes.name: Green anaconda
nodes.desc: A heavy water snake that ambushes capybaras, fish and other snakes.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Fuels the canopy, where most of the forest's growth happens, leaving the floor in deep shade.

nodes.name: Rain & river floods
nodes.desc: Daily rain and yearly river floods carry nutrients and open the forest to fish.

nodes.name: Nutrient-poor soil
nodes.desc: Heavy rain washes minerals out, so most nutrients are held in living plants and leaf litter.

nodes.name: Fungi & termites
nodes.desc: Break down leaf litter and fallen wood in weeks, so nutrients return to roots quickly.
